analysis.one_liner: Requires Congress to vote to approve major federal regulations before they can take effect.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced with 29 Republican cosponsors and placed on the Senate calendar in February 2023, but it never received a hearing or a vote before the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would flip how major federal regulations work. Today, an agency writes a rule and it takes effect unless Congress votes to reject it. Under this bill, any 'major' rule — one costing the economy $100 million or more a year, or raising costs or prices significantly — would take effect only if both chambers of Congress passed a resolution approving it. If Congress did not act within 70 working days, the rule would die, and it could not be brought back in the same Congress.
analysis.who_benefits: Large companies subject to major federal rules — in energy, manufacturing, finance, pharmaceuticals, and elsewhere — would gain the most, because in a divided Congress most major rules would fail to win approval and would lapse by default. Supporters also argue ordinary people gain accountability, since the elected Congress would have to vote on every big rule rather than leaving it to unelected agency staff.

how_it_helps.text: The bill classifies a rule as 'major' if it has an annual economic effect of $100 million or more, causes a major increase in costs or prices for consumers, industries, or governments, or significantly affects competition, employment, or investment; a major rule can take effect only after Congress enacts a joint resolution of approval.

If Congress does not pass an approval resolution within 70 session or legislative days, the rule is deemed not approved and never takes effect, and no new approval resolution for the same rule may be considered in that Congress.

The bill's stated purpose is accountability: Congress has excessively delegated legislative power to agencies, and requiring a recorded vote would make Congress answerable for the rules imposed on the public.

The bill guarantees each approval resolution a floor vote: committees must act within 15 days or be discharged, Senate debate is limited to two hours with no amendments allowed, and passage votes are mandatory by fixed deadlines.

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary people would bear the cost when protections stall: rules on clean air and water, workplace safety, food safety, consumer financial protections, and drug safety routinely cross the $100 million threshold, and under this bill each one would need affirmative approval from a Congress that often cannot pass anything contested. Agencies would also need to build a record for Congress and wait out the 70-day clock before any major rule could protect anyone.
analysis.who_pays_short: People who rely on federal protections

drawbacks.text: The default outcome is death: a major rule takes effect only if Congress affirmatively approves it within 70 days, and in a divided or narrowly split Congress the realistic result is that most contested major rules — including safety, health, and consumer protections — would never take effect.
If an approval resolution fails to pass in time, no new resolution on the same rule may be considered for the rest of that Congress, so a rule cannot simply be rescheduled and revoted.
The bill removes most court oversight: no determination or omission under the new process may be reviewed by a judge, with a narrow exception for whether an agency completed the required paperwork.

The emergency escape valve is limited: the President may let a major rule take effect for only one 90-day period at a time in cases of imminent threat to health or safety, criminal enforcement, national security, or trade-agreement obligations.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The accountability argument is real: it is a legitimate complaint that Congress writes vague laws and lets agencies fill in the details without a recorded vote. But the bill's design, not its goal, is the problem. Because approval must pass both chambers and be signed within 70 working days, and the default is that a rule dies, the practical effect in ordinary congresses would be a blanket freeze on major regulation — a broad structural win for regulated industries achieved rule by rule, without ever having to vote against a single protection. A design that required a vote but preserved a workable default would have achieved the accountability without the freeze.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in January 2023, read twice, and placed on the Senate's calendar, and then it simply sat there — no committee ever took it up, and no vote ever happened before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Rand Paul introduced the bill in the Senate on January 31, 2023.
It was read a second time on February 1, 2023 and placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders as Calendar No. 9, a step short of floor consideration.
Twenty-nine of the Senate's 49 Republicans cosponsored the bill; no Democrat or independent did.
No committee assignment, hearing, or floor vote is recorded in the action history through the end of the 118th Congress on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The outcome preserved the status quo: executive agencies keep their existing authority to issue major rules without a congressional vote, and the business coalition that sought the change got nothing. People who rely on federal protections are no worse off than before, though they also got no new accountability mechanism.

for.name: Sen. Rand Paul
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on January 31, 2023 and placed it in the Senate record with the first Republican cosponsors.

for.name: 29 of 49 Senate Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, joining the initial group of 22 sponsors and cosponsors named on introduction.

for.name: U.S. Chamber of Commerce and allied business lobbies
for.what_they_did: Have publicly supported the REINS Act across multiple Congresses as their top regulatory priority.

against.name: Chuck Schumer
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the floor for a vote; after it was placed on the calendar in February 2023, it received no floor action for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Senate Democrats and Democratic-leaning independents
against.what_they_did: Provided no cosponsors; not one Democratic or independent senator signed onto the bill.

against.name: Public Citizen and allied consumer, labor, and environmental groups
against.what_they_did: Have publicly opposed the REINS Act across multiple Congresses, arguing it would gut protections on health, safety, and the environment.

sides.party_line_note: All 29 cosponsors were Republicans and no Democrat or independent signed on, though the bill never reached a roll-call vote that would show a party breakdown on the merits.

industries.industry: Large regulated corporations (energy, chemicals, manufacturing, finance, pharmaceuticals)
industries.note: These firms bear most of the cost of rules that cross the $100 million threshold. Under the bill, such a rule would take effect only if a divided Congress affirmatively approved it within 70 working days — in practice handing regulated industries a way to stop major rules without ever casting a public vote against them.

Agencies would lose the ability to put major protections in place without a congressional approval vote, and their determinations would be largely shielded from judicial review under the new process. Their institutional interest here runs alongside the public's interest in working protections.

industries.industry: Public-health, environmental, and consumer advocacy groups
industries.note: The rules these groups push for — clean air, workplace and food safety, consumer finance — routinely qualify as major, so nearly all of their agenda would require congressional approval to take effect at all.
